claim: Drosophila Vps29 is predicted to encode a 182 amino-acid protein that is 93% similar (83% identical) to human VPS29.
source: Drosophila Vps29 is predicted to encode a 182 amino-acid protein that is 93% similar (83% identical) to human VPS29.
evidence: This is a direct statement in the manuscript comparing Drosophila and human Vps29 protein sequences.

claim: Vps291 is a homozygous viable allele.
source: Unexpectedly, Vps291 was homozygous viable, whereas both Vps35 and Vps26 mutants are lethal (Franch-Marro et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript directly states that Vps291 homozygotes are viable, contrasting with lethality of other retromer component mutants.

claim: Vps291 homozygotes are recovered at ratios below Mendelian expectation.
source: Although viable, Vps291 homozygotes are recovered at ratios below Mendelian expectation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 1—figure supplement 1A showing the data.

claim: Vps291 mutant flies exhibit a modestly reduced survival (~50–60 days versus ~75 days for controls).
source: Notably, Vps291 mutant flies exhibit a modestly reduced survival (~50–60 days versus ~75 days for controls), and this result was confirmed when Vps291 animals were crossed to the deficiency, Df(2L)Exel6004 (Figure 1D).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific survival data and references Figure 1D showing survival curves.

claim: The reduced survival in Vps29 null animals was rescued by a 23 kb P[acman] bacterial artificial chromosome containing the Vps29 genomic locus.
source: The reduced survival seen in Vps29 null animals was also rescued by a 23 kb P[acman] bacterial artificial chromosome (Venken et al., 2009) containing the Vps29 genomic locus, establishing specificity.
evidence: The manuscript states that genomic rescue restored survival, demonstrating specificity of the phenotype.

claim: Loss of Vps29 disrupts light-induced depolarization in 10-day-old flies.
source: Loss of either Vps29 or Vps35 disrupted light-induced depolarization (arrow) in 10-day-old flies.
evidence: The manuscript describes ERG phenotypes shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Raising flies in the dark restored ERG depolarization but not the transients in Vps29 mutants.
source: Raising flies in the dark restored ERG depolarization, but not the transients, indicating persistent defects in synaptic transmission.
evidence: The manuscript describes differential rescue of ERG components by dark-rearing, shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Vps29 mutants show progressive decline in on- and off-transient potentials following rapid light stimulation.
source: Indeed, we documented a progressive decline in the on- and off-transient potentials following rapid stimulation, and consistent results were also obtained using the ey3.5-FLP driver (Mehta et al., 2005), which selectively targets presynaptic neurons (Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The manuscript describes ERG run-down phenotype with rapid stimulation, shown in Figure 1H.

claim: The ERG run-down phenotype is characteristic of mutants that disrupt synaptic vesicle recycling.
source: This 'run-down' phenotype is characteristic of mutants that disrupt synaptic vesicle recycling (Harris and Littleton, 2015), suggesting that retromer is required for this process.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the run-down phenotype based on published literature.

claim: Pan-neuronal overexpression of Vps35 partially restored synaptic transmission in Vps291 homozygous animals.
source: Surprisingly, we also found that pan-neuronal overexpression of Vps35 (nSyb>Vps35) partially restored synaptic transmission in Vps291 homozygous animals.
evidence: The manuscript describes rescue experiments shown in Figure 1I.

claim: Vps291 homozygous larvae show a modest but significant increase in synaptic bouton numbers at the NMJ.
source: Indeed, NMJ preparations from Vps291 homozygous larvae revealed a modest but significant increase in synaptic bouton numbers, consistent with synaptic overgrowth (Figure 2A).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantification of NMJ bouton numbers shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Both amplitude and frequency of NMJ miniature excitatory junction potentials (mEJPs) were unaffected following loss of Vps29.
source: However, both amplitude and frequency of NMJ miniature excitatory junction potentials (mEJPs) were unaffected following loss of Vps29 (Figure 2B).
evidence: The manuscript reports electrophysiology data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Excitatory junction potentials (EJPs) were preserved in Vps29 mutants.
source: Similarly, excitatory junction potentials (EJPs) were also preserved (Figure 2C).
evidence: The manuscript reports electrophysiology data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: High-frequency stimulation (10 Hz for 10 min) provoked a marked synaptic depression at the Vps291 NMJ.
source: However, high-frequency stimulation (10 Hz for 10 min) provoked a marked synaptic depression at the Vps291 NMJ (Figure 2D).
evidence: The manuscript reports electrophysiology data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: NMJs from Vps291 homozygous animals show significantly reduced FM 1-43 dye uptake.
source: However, NMJs from either Vps291 or Vps35MH20 homozygous animals significantly reduced FM dye uptake.
evidence: The manuscript reports FM dye uptake assay results shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Vps29 null adults do not show obvious morphological defects or apparent evidence of neurodegeneration in the brains of 45-day-old animals based on hematoxylin and eosin staining.
source: Except for the aforementioned retinal requirement, we did not observe obvious morphological defects or apparent evidence of neurodegeneration in the brains of 45-day-old Vps291/Df adults based on hematoxylin and eosin staining of paraffin sections (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript describes histological analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Climbing ability significantly declined with aging in Vps29 null animals.
source: Although locomotor behavior was normal in newly eclosed Vps29 null adults, climbing ability significantly declined with aging (Figure 3A).
evidence: The manuscript reports locomotor assay results shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Vps35 and Vps26 protein levels are normal in the absence of Vps29.
source: However, Vps35 and Vps26 protein levels were unaffected in Vps29 null animals (either Vps291 homozygotes or Vps291/Df), based on western blots from either whole larvae or adult Drosophila heads (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C), including from 30-day-old animals.
evidence: The manuscript reports western blot data shown in Figure 3C and supplemental figures.

claim: Vps35 and Vps26 remain tightly associated in the absence of Vps29.
source: Furthermore, we confirmed that Vps35 and Vps26 remain tightly associated in the absence of Vps29, based on coimmunoprecipitation assays (Figure 3D).
evidence: The manuscript reports coimmunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: In Vps291 homozygous animals, Vps35 showed a striking redistribution, shifting from neuropil to enrichment in soma, and forming large perinuclear puncta.
source: However, in Vps291 homozygous animals, Vps35 showed a striking redistribution, shifting from neuropil to enrichment in soma, and forming large perinuclear puncta (Figure 4C).
evidence: The manuscript describes immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Vps35 was mislocalized in brains from 1-day-old adults and this result did not significantly change with aging.
source: Moreover, Vps35 was mislocalized in brains from 1-day-old adults and this result did not significantly change with aging.
evidence: The manuscript states that mislocalization occurs early and persists.

claim: In Vps291 homozygotes, both Vps35 and Vps26 accumulated in the lamina cortex and staining was attenuated in the lamina neuropil.
source: Specifically, in Vps291 homozygotes, both Vps35 and Vps26 accumulated in the lamina cortex and staining was attenuated in the lamina neuropil.
evidence: The manuscript describes immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: In the adult brain of Vps291 homozygotes, the Rab7 signal appeared strongly increased and was restricted to a somatic, perinuclear pattern with relative depletion from neuropil.
source: Indeed, in the adult brain of Vps291 homozygotes, the Rab7 signal appeared strongly increased and was restricted to a somatic, perinuclear pattern with relative depletion from neuropil.
evidence: The manuscript describes immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Mislocalized Vps35 strongly costained with perinuclear Rab7 and Arl8.
source: Importantly, mislocalized Vps35 strongly costained with perinuclear Rab7 and Arl8, suggesting enrichment at the late endosome and/or lysosome.
evidence: The manuscript describes colocalization data shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Rab7 protein is increased in Vps291 homozygotes or Vps291/Df on western blots.
source: On western blots, we documented an increase in Rab7 protein in either Vps291 homozygotes or Vps291/Df (Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: The manuscript reports western blot data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The constitutively active, GTP-locked Rab7Q67L protein was present at higher levels than wildtype or GDP-locked forms.
source: We found that the constitutively active, GTP-locked Rab7Q67L protein was present at higher levels (Figure 4G and Figure 4—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: The manuscript reports western blot data shown in Figure 4G comparing different Rab7 forms.

claim: Removing one copy of Rab7 partially rescued the age-dependent locomotor impairment in Vps291/Df animals.
source: Indeed, although complete loss-of-function for Rab7 is lethal, removing one copy (Rab7Gal4-KO/+) (Cherry et al., 2013) partially rescued the age-dependent locomotor impairment and synaptic transmission defects manifest in Vps291/Df animals (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: The manuscript reports genetic interaction data shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: Reduction of Rab7 restored synaptic vesicle endocytosis at the larval NMJ in Vps291 homozygotes based on the FM 1-43 dye uptake assay.
source: Reduction of Rab7 also restored synaptic vesicle endocytosis at the larval NMJ in Vps291 homozygotes, based on the FM 1–43 dye uptake assay (Figure 5C).
evidence: The manuscript reports FM dye uptake assay results shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Pan-neuronal overexpression of dTBC1D5 normalized Rab7 protein levels in Vps29 mutants.
source: Consistent with our model, pan-neuronal overexpression of dTBC1D5 (nsyb>dTBC1D5) normalized Rab7 protein levels (Figure 5D) and partially rescued the synaptic transmission defect in Vps29 mutants (Figure 5E).
evidence: The manuscript reports western blot and ERG data shown in Figure 5D,E.

claim: Vps29L152E failed to complement Vps291, causing age-dependent photoreceptor synaptic transmission defects and locomotor impairment.
source: Vps29L152E failed to complement Vps291 (Figure 5F–H and Figure 5—figure supplement 1), causing age-dependent photoreceptor synaptic transmission defects and locomotor impairment.
evidence: The manuscript reports complementation test results shown in Figure 5F-H.

claim: Vps29L152E was expressed at higher levels and Rab7 was also increased.
source: Moreover, Vps29L152E was expressed at higher levels and Rab7 was also increased, as in Vps291.
evidence: The manuscript reports western blot data shown in Figure 5H and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Glucosylceramide accumulates in Vps291 homozygous photoreceptors.
source: We confirmed that glucosylceramide similarly accumulates in Vps291 homozygous photoreceptors (Figure 6A), consistent with the retinal degeneration phenotype.
evidence: The manuscript reports immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Mature CTSL levels were normal and mature CTSD was increased in adult head homogenates from 1-day-old Vps291/Df animals.
source: We detected normal levels of mature CTSL and increased mature CTSD in adult head homogenates from 1-day-old Vps291/Df animals (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript reports western blot data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: In 30-day-old animals, the uncleaved proforms of both cathepsins were sharply increased.
source: However, in 30-day-old animals, we found that the uncleaved proforms of both cathepsins were sharply increased, consistent with progressive lysosomal dysfunction with aging.
evidence: The manuscript reports western blot data shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: At 45 days, Vps29 mutants showed evidence of accelerated autophagic failure, with more significant elevation of both p62 and Atg8, and accumulation of polyubiquitinated proteins.
source: Interestingly, however, at more extreme ages (45 days), Vps29 mutants showed evidence of accelerated autophagic failure, with more significant elevation of both p62 and Atg8, and accumulation of polyubiquitinated proteins (Figure 6C).
evidence: The manuscript reports western blot data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Reduction of Rab7 improved autophagic clearance in Vps29 mutant brains.
source: Notably, reduction of Rab7 (Rab7Gal4-KO/+) improved autophagic clearance in Vps29 mutant brains.
evidence: The manuscript reports western blot data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Retinal TEM revealed normal numbers and morphology of photoreceptors in 30-day-old Vps291/Df animals.
source: Indeed, retinal TEM revealed normal numbers and morphology of photoreceptors; however, we documented significantly increased numbers of lysosomes, multivesicular bodies, and autophagic vacuoles.
evidence: The manuscript reports TEM data shown in Figure 7A-C.

claim: Lysosomes in Vps29 mutant retinae were frequently aberrantly enlarged and filled with granular, electron-dense material.
source: Further, lysosomes were frequently aberrantly enlarged and filled with granular, electron-dense material.
evidence: The manuscript describes TEM observations shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Vps29 mutant synaptic terminals in the lamina appeared unremarkable with normal synapse numbers and size.
source: Interestingly, although synaptic transmission is disrupted in these animals (i.e. reduced ERG on/off transients), Vps29 mutant synaptic terminals in the lamina appeared unremarkable. We observed normal synapse numbers and size, nor did we detect any other apparent evidence of synaptic degeneration.
evidence: The manuscript describes TEM observations shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Significantly increased numbers of aberrant lysosomal structures (multilamellar bodies) were found in Vps29 mutant brain cortical regions.
source: Consistent with findings in the retina, we discovered significantly increased numbers of aberrant lysosomal structures (multilamellar bodies) in Vps29 mutants.
evidence: The manuscript reports TEM data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: VPS35 is a retromer core protein.
source: Mutations in VPS35—encoding a retromer core protein—are a rare cause of familial Parkinson's disease (Vilariño-Güell et al., 2011; Zimprich et al., 2011)
evidence: The manuscript states this as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Mutations in VPS35 are a rare cause of familial Parkinson's disease.
source: Mutations in VPS35—encoding a retromer core protein—are a rare cause of familial Parkinson's disease (Vilariño-Güell et al., 2011; Zimprich et al., 2011)
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature establishing this link.

claim: Retromer has been linked to endocytic trafficking and processing of the Amyloid Precursor Protein and Tau in Alzheimer's disease.
source: and retromer has also been linked to endocytic trafficking and processing of the Amyloid Precursor Protein and Tau in Alzheimer's disease (Muhammad et al., 2008; Vagnozzi et al., 2019; Wen et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature establishing this link.

claim: The heterotrimeric core proteins of the retromer, VPS35, VPS26, and VPS29, are highly conserved among eukaryotes.
source: Originally discovered in the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae (Seaman et al., 1998), the heterotrimeric core proteins of the retromer, VPS35, VPS26, and VPS29, are highly conserved among eukaryotes (Koumandou et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature establishing conservation.

claim: Retromer components are broadly expressed, including in the invertebrate nervous system and throughout the mammalian brain.
source: Retromer components are broadly expressed, including in the invertebrate nervous system (Inoshita et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2014) and throughout the mammalian brain (Appel et al., 2018; Tsika et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature on retromer expression patterns.

claim: In murine neurons, retromer is present in both axons and dendrites, and at the synapse.
source: In murine neurons, retromer is present in both axons and dendrites, and at the synapse (Munsie et al., 2015; Tsika et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature on retromer localization.

claim: Post-synaptically, retromer appears important for trafficking of AMPA, β2 adrenergic, and perhaps other neurotransmitter receptors to the dendritic membrane.
source: Post-synaptically, retromer appears important for trafficking of AMPA, β2 adrenergic, and perhaps other neurotransmitter receptors to the dendritic membrane (Choy et al., 2014; Munsie et al., 2015; Temkin et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature on retromer function at the postsynapse.

claim: In rat mesencephalic cultures, retromer participates in pre-synaptic dopamine transporter trafficking.
source: In rat mesencephalic cultures, retromer also participates in pre-synaptic dopamine transporter trafficking (Wu et al., 2017)
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature on retromer function at the presynapse.

claim: Studies of Vps35 at the Drosophila neuromuscular junction suggest a requirement for synaptic vesicle recycling.
source: and studies of Vps35 at the Drosophila neuromuscular junction suggest a requirement for synaptic vesicle recycling (Inoshita et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature on Vps35 function at the NMJ.

claim: Vps35-deficient mice exhibit both defective hippocampal neurotransmission and dopaminergic insufficiency.
source: Vps35-deficient mice exhibit both defective hippocampal neurotransmission (Muhammad et al., 2008) and dopaminergic insufficiency (Tang et al., 2015a; Tang et al., 2015b), leading to impairments in memory and locomotion, respectively.
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature on Vps35 mouse models.

claim: In the absence of retromer, many protein cargoes are misdirected to the lysosome.
source: In the absence of retromer, many protein cargoes are misdirected to the lysosome (Burd and Cullen, 2014; Lucas and Hierro, 2017; Wang and Bellen, 2015), potentially overwhelming degradative capacity, leading to lysosomal expansion and cellular stress.
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature on retromer function in cargo sorting.

claim: In the Drosophila retina, loss-of-function for Vps35 or Vps26 results in accumulation of Rhodopsin-1 (Rh1) within photoreceptors, ultimately causing neuronal dysfunction and loss.
source: For example, in the Drosophila retina, loss-of-function for Vps35 or Vps26 results in accumulation of the visual pigment, Rhodopsin-1 (Rh1), within photoreceptors, ultimately causing neuronal dysfunction and loss (Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature on retromer function in the retina.

claim: Ablation of VPS35 in the mouse germline is embryonic lethal.
source: Ablation of VPS35 in the mouse germline is embryonic lethal (Wen et al., 2011)
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature on VPS35 mouse knockout.

claim: Both Vps35 and Vps26 have essential developmental requirements in Drosophila.
source: and both Vps35 and Vps26 similarly have essential developmental requirements in Drosophila (de Vreede et al., 2014; Franch-Marro et al., 2008; Pocha et al., 2011; Starble and Pokrywka, 2018; Strutt et al., 2019; Wang and Bellen, 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature on Vps35 and Vps26 requirements in Drosophila.

claim: VPS29 binds the VPS35 C-terminus.
source: VPS29 binds the VPS35 C-terminus (Collins et al., 2005; Hierro et al., 2007; Kovtun et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature on VPS29-VPS35 interaction.

claim: Deletion of Vps29 in yeast or Caenorhabditis elegans phenocopies Vps35 loss-of-function.
source: Deletion of Vps29 in yeast or Caenorhabditis elegans phenocopies Vps35 loss-of-function (Lorenowicz et al., 2014; Seaman et al., 1997).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature on Vps29 function in other organisms.

claim: In mammalian epithelial cell culture, reducing VPS29 results in apparent destabilization and degradation of both VPS35 and VPS26.
source: In mammalian epithelial cell culture, reducing VPS29 results in apparent destabilization and degradation of both VPS35 and VPS26 (Fuse et al., 2015; Jimenez-Orgaz et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature on VPS29 function in cell culture.

claim: Pharmacological chaperones targeting the VPS35-VPS29 interface can stabilize the complex and enhance retromer function.
source: Reciprocally, pharmacological chaperones targeting the VPS35-VPS29 interface can stabilize the complex and enhance retromer function (Mecozzi et al., 2014; Young et al., 2018; Lin et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature on pharmacological modulation of retromer.

claim: Vps29 is required for retromer localization via a Rab7- and TBC1D5-dependent regulatory pathway.
source: Unexpectedly, Vps29 loss did not affect the expression or stability of other retromer components but influenced their localization via a Rab7- and TBC1D5-dependent regulatory pathway.
evidence: This is a summary statement in the abstract supported by multiple experiments in the manuscript.

claim: With aging, retromer insufficiency triggers progressive endolysosomal dysfunction, with ultrastructural evidence of impaired substrate clearance and lysosomal stress.
source: With aging, retromer insufficiency triggers progressive endolysosomal dysfunction, with ultrastructural evidence of impaired substrate clearance and lysosomal stress.
evidence: This is a summary statement in the abstract supported by multiple experiments in the manuscript.

source: Vps29 is required for age-dependent retinal function

source: Retromer regulates synaptic vesicle endocytosis and recycling

source: Vps29 interacts with Rab7 and TBC1D5
evidence: This is a section heading summarizing findings presented in that section.

source: Loss of Vps29 causes lysosomal dysfunction during aging

source: VPS29 is required for retromer recruitment via Rab7 and TBC1D5

source: The retromer and endolysosomal trafficking in neurons

source: In neurons, the retromer core Vp26-Vps35-Vps29 is recruited by Rab7 to the endosomal membrane.
evidence: This is stated in the model shown in Figure 8.

claim: Vps29 engages TBC1D5, which promotes inactivation of Rab7 and release of Vps35.
source: Vps29 engages TBC1D5, which promotes inactivation of Rab7 and release of Vps35.
evidence: This is stated in the model shown in Figure 8.

source: In the absence of Vps29, the residual retromer complex is trapped at the endosomal membrane.

claim: Vps35 is recruited to endosomal membranes by the Rab7 GTPase.
source: Based on cell culture studies, Vps35 is recruited to endosomal membranes by the Rab7 GTPase (Seaman et al., 2009)
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature on Vps35 recruitment.

claim: VPS29 knockdown has been previously suggested to increase GTP-bound, activated Rab7.
source: and VPS29 knockdown has been previously suggested to increase GTP-bound, activated Rab7 (Jimenez-Orgaz et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature on VPS29 and Rab7.

claim: VPS29 regulates Rab7 activity via recruitment of the GTPase-activating protein (GAP), TBC1D5.
source: In mammalian cell culture studies, VPS29 regulates Rab7 activity via recruitment of the GTPase-activating protein (GAP), TBC1D5 (Jia et al., 2016; Seaman et al., 2009).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature on VPS29-TBC1D5 interaction.

claim: Drosophila has a single ortholog of TBC1D5 that is well-conserved (28% identity/47% similarity).
source: Drosophila has a single ortholog of TBC1D5 that is well-conserved (28% identity/47% similarity) (Gramates et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript states this based on database information.

claim: Mutation of the conserved Vps29 L152 residue disrupts the interaction with TBC1D5 in mammalian cells.
source: mutation of this conserved residue has been shown to disrupt the interaction with TBC1D5 in mammalian cells (Jia et al., 2016; Jimenez-Orgaz et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature on the L152E mutation.

claim: Loss of Vps35 in the Drosophila retina causes accumulation of ceramide lipid species.
source: In the Drosophila retina, besides aberrant trafficking of Rh1 (Wang et al., 2014), loss of Vps35 causes accumulation of ceramide lipid species (Lin et al., 2018), which contributes to lysosomal expansion, cellular stress, and ultimately photoreceptor loss.
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature on Vps35 and ceramides.

claim: Lysosomal dysfunction commonly leads to reduced levels of mature cathepsins and increased levels of the immature proforms.
source: These enzymes are each synthesized as propeptides in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and become active following cleavage in the acidic, lysosomal milieu. Lysosomal dysfunction therefore commonly leads to reduced levels of mature cathepsins and increased levels of the immature proforms (Hasanagic et al., 2015; Li et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature on cathepsin processing.

claim: Substrate degradation is triggered when Atg8-decorated autophagosomes fuse with lysosomes, leading to turnover of Ref(2)P/p62 and concomitant clearance of polyubiquitinated proteins.
source: Substrate degradation is triggered when Atg8-decorated autophagosomes fuse with lysosomes, leading to turnover of Ref(2)P/p62 and concomitant clearance of polyubiquitinated proteins.
evidence: The manuscript describes established autophagy mechanisms.

claim: Retromer dysfunction has been linked to pathogenesis of Parkinson's and Alzheimer's disease.
source: Retromer dysfunction has been linked to pathogenesis of Parkinson's and Alzheimer's disease (Small and Petsko, 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature on retromer in neurodegeneration.

claim: In both Parkinson's and Alzheimer's disease, synaptic dysfunction is an early pathologic feature, and lysosomal autophagy is also strongly implicated.
source: In both neurodegenerative disorders, synaptic dysfunction is an early pathologic feature, and lysosomal autophagy is also strongly implicated (Ihara et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature on synaptic and lysosomal dysfunction in neurodegeneration.

claim: Variants at numerous genetic loci related to endocytic trafficking and synaptic maintenance have been discovered as risk factors for Alzheimer's disease.
source: In fact, variants at numerous other genetic loci related to endocytic trafficking and synaptic maintenance have been discovered as risk factors for Alzheimer's disease (BIN1, PICALM, CD2AP, SORL1) (Karch et al., 2014)
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature on Alzheimer's disease genetics.

claim: Variants at genetic loci related to endocytic trafficking have been discovered as risk factors for Parkinson's disease.
source: and Parkinson's disease (SNCA, LRRK2, SH3GL2/EndoA, RAB7L1) (Soukup et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature on Parkinson's disease genetics.

claim: Genetic links have recently emerged between Parkinson's disease and lysosomal storage disorders.
source: Genetic links have also recently emerged between Parkinson's disease and lysosomal storage disorders, comprising a heterogeneous group of recessive disorders arising from defects in lysosomal biogenesis and/or function (Ysselstein et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature on Parkinson's disease and lysosomal storage disorders.

claim: Retromer participates in the trafficking of lysosomal hydrolases.
source: Importantly, retromer participates in the trafficking of lysosomal hydrolases (Cui et al., 2019; Seaman et al., 1997)
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature on retromer function.

claim: Synaptic dysfunction may be an early manifestation in lysosomal storage disorders.
source: Based on mouse models, synaptic dysfunction may be an early manifestation in lysosomal storage disorders similar to Vps29 mutant flies (Mitter et al., 2003; Ohara et al., 2004; Sambri et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature on lysosomal storage disorder models.

claim: Aberrant lysosomal morphology has been described in both Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease models.
source: Aberrant lysosomal morphology has also been described in both Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease models (Giasson et al., 2002; Stokin et al., 2005) and in human postmortem brain (García-Sanz et al., 2018; Piras et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature on lysosomal pathology in neurodegeneration.

claim: Small molecule chaperones that bind Vps29 are available for therapeutic manipulation in neurodegenerative disease.
source: Targeting the retromer for therapeutic manipulation in neurodegenerative disease is one promising approach, given the availability of small molecule chaperones that bind Vps29 (Mecozzi et al., 2014; Vagnozzi et al., 2019; Young et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature on pharmacological approaches.

claim: The entire Vps29 coding sequence was replaced by the ywing2+ marker gene in the Vps291 allele.
source: In the resulting mutant, Vps291, the entire coding sequence was replaced by the visible marker gene, ywing2+ (Figure 1A).
evidence: The manuscript describes the molecular lesion shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Loss of the Vps29 genomic sequence in null animals was confirmed by PCR and sequencing of the insertional breakpoints.
source: Loss of the Vps29 genomic sequence in null animals was confirmed by PCR (Figure 1B) and sequencing of the insertional breakpoints
evidence: The manuscript describes molecular confirmation shown in Figure 1B.

claim: No Vps29 protein was detected using an anti-Vps29 antibody on western blots from fly head homogenates of Vps291 animals.
source: and we were not able to detect any protein using an anti-Vps29 antibody on western blots from fly head homogenates (Figure 1C).
evidence: The manuscript describes western blot data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Viable Vps291 animals lacking both maternal and zygotic protein were recovered when crossing homozygous females to heterozygous males.
source: We also recovered viable Vps291 animals lacking both maternal and zygotic protein when crossing homozygous females to heterozygous males.
evidence: The manuscript describes genetic crosses demonstrating lack of maternal requirement.

claim: Human VPS29 is capable of functional substitution in Drosophila.
source: Finally, similar rescue was observed when expressing three alternate human Vps29 isoforms, consistent with functional conservation.
evidence: The manuscript reports rescue experiments shown in Figure 1I.

claim: Vps29 is dispensable for retromer function during embryogenesis and development.
source: In sum, whereas Vps29 appears dispensable for retromer function during embryogenesis and development, these studies reveal a requirement in the aging nervous system for phototransduction and synaptic transmission.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the viability of Vps29 mutants and their age-dependent phenotypes.

claim: Vps29 is required in the aging nervous system for phototransduction and synaptic transmission.
source: In sum, whereas Vps29 appears dispensable for retromer function during embryogenesis and development, these studies reveal a requirement in the aging nervous system for phototransduction and synaptic transmission.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on multiple experiments showing age-dependent phenotypes.

claim: Vps35 is present at both the NMJ pre- and post-synapse.
source: Based on previous work, Vps35 is present at both the NMJ pre- and post-synapse, and loss of Vps35 causes synaptic terminal overgrowth and altered neurophysiology suggestive of synaptic vesicle recycling defects (Inoshita et al., 2017; Korolchuk et al., 2007; Malik et al., 2015; Walsh et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature on Vps35 localization and function at the NMJ.

claim: Vps29 is neither required for spontaneous nor evoked synaptic vesicle release.
source: These results suggest that Vps29 is neither required for spontaneous nor evoked synaptic vesicle release.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on normal mEJP and EJP data shown in Figure 2B,C.

claim: The NMJ synaptic run-down phenotype is characteristic of mutants causing defective endocytosis.
source: The NMJ synaptic run-down phenotype is characteristic of mutants causing defective endocytosis (Bellen et al., 2010; Verstreken et al., 2002; Winther et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature on synaptic run-down phenotypes.

claim: Retromer may regulate the trafficking of a key factor required for synaptic membrane endocytosis and/or replenishing of the vesicle pool from synaptic endosomes.
source: First, retromer may regulate the trafficking of a key factor required for synaptic membrane endocytosis and/or replenishing of the vesicle pool from synaptic endosomes.
evidence: This is a speculative model proposed in the discussion.

claim: Vps29-related synaptic dysfunction may be related to progressive lysosomal dysfunction.
source: Second, Vps29-related synaptic dysfunction may instead be related, more broadly, to progressive lysosomal dysfunction.
evidence: This is a speculative model proposed in the discussion.

claim: Recent studies have linked synaptic endosomes, lysosomes, and autophagosomes to presynaptic proteostasis, including during vesicle recycling and release.
source: In fact, recent studies have linked synaptic endosomes, lysosomes, and autophagosomes to presynaptic proteostasis, including during vesicle recycling and release (Jin et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature on synaptic proteostasis.

claim: TBC1D24 (Skywalker in Drosophila) regulates synaptic vesicle recycling and quality control via a sorting endosome at NMJ terminals.
source: For example, another Rab GTPase activating protein, TBC1D24—Skywalker in Drosophila—has been shown to regulate synaptic vesicle recycling and quality control via a sorting endosome at NMJ terminals (Fernandes et al., 2014; Uytterhoeven et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature on TBC1D24/Skywalker function.

claim: Raising Vps29 or Vps35 mutants in the dark rescued retinal degeneration but not synaptic transmission defects.
source: Interestingly, in the Drosophila visual system, we found that raising Vps29 or Vps35 mutants in the dark rescued retinal degeneration but not synaptic transmission defects, consistent with an uncoupling of retromer requirements in these two spatially distinct processes.
evidence: The manuscript describes differential rescue by dark-rearing.

claim: Synaptic endolysosomal trafficking and function can be regulated independently from that of the neuronal soma.
source: Thus, it is possible—if not likely—that synaptic endolysosomal trafficking and function can be regulated independently from that of the neuronal soma.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the differential rescue data.

claim: Retromer components are present at synaptic terminals in mouse primary neuronal culture.
source: Retromer components are present at synaptic terminals in mouse primary neuronal culture (Munsie et al., 2015; Vazquez-Sanchez et al., 2018) and in cortical synaptosome preparations (Tsika et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature on retromer localization in mammalian neurons.

claim: Variants at genetic loci related to endocytic trafficking and synaptic maintenance have been discovered as risk factors for Alzheimer's disease, including BIN1, PICALM, CD2AP, and SORL1.
source: In fact, variants at numerous other genetic loci related to endocytic trafficking and synaptic maintenance have been discovered as risk factors for Alzheimer's disease (BIN1, PICALM, CD2AP, SORL1) (Karch et al., 2014)
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature on Alzheimer's disease genetics.

claim: Variants at genetic loci related to endocytic trafficking have been discovered as risk factors for Parkinson's disease, including SNCA, LRRK2, SH3GL2/EndoA, and RAB7L1.
source: and Parkinson's disease (SNCA, LRRK2, SH3GL2/EndoA, RAB7L1) (Soukup et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature on Parkinson's disease genetics.

claim: Lysosomal storage disorders are characterized by the accumulation of undigested substrates and lysosomal expansion.
source: These disorders, which can include neurodegenerative features, are characterized by the accumulation of undigested substrates and lysosomal expansion (e.g. glucosylceramide in Gaucher's disease).
evidence: The manuscript describes characteristics of lysosomal storage disorders.

claim: The viability of Vps29 mutants is unexpected compared to other retromer subunits.
source: By contrast, the viability of Vps29 mutants as well as our finding of a more selective, regulatory role for Vps29 in complex localization is unexpected.
evidence: This is an interpretation comparing Vps29 to Vps35 and Vps26 requirements.

claim: Vps35 can weakly bind TBC1D5.
source: Since Vps35 can weakly bind TBC1D5 (Jia et al., 2016), it may be capable of inactivating Rab7, compensating in part for the absence of Vps29.
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature on Vps35-TBC1D5 interaction.

claim: The specific requirement(s) for Vps29 may be context dependent, varying with cell-type and/or specific cargo.
source: Importantly, these data suggest that the specific requirement(s) for Vps29—and by extension, retromer activity—may be context dependent, varying with cell-type (e.g. neuron) and/or specific cargo (e.g. Rh1, ceramides, or others).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the partial phenotypes observed.

claim: Vps29 may participate in other endosomal sorting machinery besides retromer, such as the 'retriever' complex.
source: It is also possible that tissue- or species-specific differences might relate to Vps29 participation in other endosomal sorting machinery besides retromer, such as the recently described 'retriever' (McNally et al., 2017); however, this complex has not yet been studied in Drosophila.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation citing published literature on the retriever complex.

claim: Neurons can initially compensate for retromer insufficiency, whereas adaptive mechanisms may breakdown during aging.
source: This result suggests that neurons can initially compensate for retromer insufficiency, whereas adaptive mechanisms may breakdown during aging.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on age-dependent phenotypes.

claim: Neuronal compensation may entail increasing capacity for substrate turnover.
source: Neuronal compensation may entail increasing capacity for substrate turnover, since we found that mature forms of CTSD and markers of autophagic flux were increased in young animals (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on western blot data.

claim: The production of critical membrane proteins dependent on retromer for recycling can be boosted, at least temporarily.
source: It is also possible that the production of critical membrane proteins dependent on retromer for recycling can be boosted, at least temporarily.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation.

claim: Aging is accompanied by reduced degradative capacity in neurons.
source: However, there is ample evidence from animal model studies that aging is accompanied by reduced degradative capacity in neurons, which may ultimately contribute to decompensation and increased proteotoxic stress (Mattson and Magnus, 2006).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature on aging and neuronal function.

claim: Loss of Vps35 but not Vps29 affected spontaneous NMJ activity, causing increased miniature excitatory junction potentials.
source: Whereas both genes appear similarly required for synaptic vesicle endocytosis, loss of Vps35 but not Vps29, also affected spontaneous NMJ activity, causing increased miniature excitatory junction potentials (Inoshita et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature and compares to current findings.

claim: ERGs revealed age-dependent, progressive decline in synaptic transmission in Vps29 mutants.
source: Interestingly, ERGs also revealed age-dependent, progressive decline in synaptic transmission.
evidence: This is based on ERG data shown in multiple figures.

claim: TEM studies of the Drosophila lamina did not reveal overt synaptic structural changes despite significant degradation of synaptic function.
source: Despite evidence of significant degradation of synaptic function with aging, TEM studies of the Drosophila lamina did not reveal overt synaptic structural changes, suggesting a more subtle, predominantly functional defect.
evidence: The manuscript describes TEM observations shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Retromer is present throughout embryonic and larval development.
source: Since retromer is present throughout embryonic and larval development, we cannot exclude the possibility of developmental defects due to Vps29 loss-of-function.
evidence: This is stated as a caveat in interpreting the results.

claim: Vps35 was mislocalized in the Vps29 mutant larval brain.
source: Indeed, Vps35 was mislocalized in the Vps29 mutant larval brain and we documented increased numbers of NMJ synaptic boutons.
evidence: The manuscript describes immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The adult brain appeared grossly normal in Vps29 mutants.
source: Nevertheless, the adult brain appeared grossly normal, and electroretinograms and climbing were unaffected in newly eclosed flies.
evidence: This is based on histology and behavioral data.

claim: Electroretinograms and climbing were unaffected in newly eclosed Vps29 mutant flies.
source: Nevertheless, the adult brain appeared grossly normal, and electroretinograms and climbing were unaffected in newly eclosed flies.
evidence: This is based on ERG and behavioral data.

claim: Retromer may directly or indirectly support vesicle recycling at the presynapse.
source: First, retromer may regulate the trafficking of a key factor required for synaptic membrane endocytosis and/or replenishing of the vesicle pool from synaptic endosomes.
evidence: This is a speculative model proposed in the discussion.

claim: Synaptic endosomes, lysosomes, and autophagosomes are linked to presynaptic proteostasis.
source: In fact, recent studies have linked synaptic endosomes, lysosomes, and autophagosomes to presynaptic proteostasis, including during vesicle recycling and release (Jin et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature on synaptic proteostasis.
